findings.title: Ec2 Imdsv1 Optional
findings.description: The current configuration has http_tokens set to 'optional', which allows IMDSv1 and makes the instance vulnerable to SSRF attacks. By changing it to 'required', we enforce the use of IMDSv2, which is more secure. This change ensures that the instance metadata service (IMDS) requires a signed token for access, reducing the risk of unauthorized access.
findings.fix_hint: Update the http_tokens value to 'required' to enforce IMDSv2 and prevent SSRF attacks

findings.title: Xentinel Hardcoded Aws Access Key
findings.description: Hardcoding sensitive credentials like AWS access keys and database passwords poses a significant security risk, as they can be exposed to unauthorized parties. Using environment variables to store these credentials helps to keep them secure and separate from the codebase. This approach also makes it easier to manage and rotate credentials across different environments.
findings.fix_hint: Use environment variables to store sensitive credentials
findings.fixed_code:
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID = os.environ['AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID']
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = os.environ['AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY']
DB_PASSWORD = os.environ['DB_PASSWORD']
STRIPE_SECRET = os.environ['STRIPE_SECRET']

findings.title: Tainted Sql String
findings.description: The original code is vulnerable to SQL injection because it directly inserts user input into the query string. By using a parameterized query, the database driver will properly escape the input, preventing malicious SQL from being executed. This fix ensures that the user_id is treated as a parameter, not part of the SQL code.
findings.cwe: CWE-704: Incorrect Type Conversion or Cast
findings.fix_hint: Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection attacks
findings.fixed_code: query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?'; result = conn.execute(query, (user_id,)).fetchall()

findings.title: Subprocess Injection
findings.description: The original code is vulnerable to command injection because it uses the shell=True argument and passes the command as a string, allowing an attacker to inject malicious commands. By passing the command and arguments as a list, we avoid the shell injection vulnerability. The fixed code uses the subprocess module with a list of arguments to safely execute the ping command.
findings.cwe: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
findings.fix_hint: Use the subprocess module with a dictionary to allowlist a set of commands and avoid shell injection by passing arguments as a list instead of a string

findings.title: Dangerous Subprocess Use
findings.description: The original code is vulnerable to command injection because it directly uses user-controlled input in the subprocess function. Using shlex.quote() to escape the input prevents malicious actors from injecting arbitrary commands. The fixed code uses the subprocess function with a list of arguments instead of a string to avoid shell injection.
findings.cwe: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
findings.fix_hint: Use the shlex library to escape user-controlled input for the subprocess function

findings.title: Subprocess Shell True
findings.description: The subprocess.check_output function is vulnerable to command injection when shell=True is used, allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary commands. By passing the command as a list of arguments with shell=False, we prevent the shell from interpreting the command and reduce the risk of injection. This change ensures that only the intended ping command is executed with the provided host argument.
findings.cwe: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
findings.fix_hint: Replace shell=True with shell=False and pass the command as a list of arguments to prevent command injection

findings.title: Path Traversal Open
findings.description: The vulnerability exists because the filename is directly used to open a file without any validation or sanitization, allowing an attacker to traverse the file system. To fix this, the filename should be validated and sanitized to prevent path traversal attacks. The provided fixed code snippet demonstrates how to replace '../' and '..\' with an empty string to prevent directory traversal.
findings.cwe: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')
findings.fix_hint: Validate and sanitize the filename to prevent path traversal attacks
findings.fixed_code: filename = request.args.get('name'); filename = filename.replace('../', '').replace('..\', ''); filename = '/var/data/' + filename; with open(filename) as f: return f.read()

findings.title: Xentinel Sql Injection Format
findings.description: The original code is vulnerable to SQL injection because it directly interpolates user input into the query string. Using parameterized queries with placeholders for user input prevents an attacker from injecting malicious SQL. The mysql library supports parameterized queries, which are used in the fixed code to securely pass user input to the query.
findings.fix_hint: Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection
findings.fixed_code: const query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?'; conn.query(query, [username, password], (err, results) => { callback(results && results.length > 0); });

findings.title: Security group allows unrestricted RDP (port 3389)
findings.description: The current security group rule allows unrestricted access to RDP on port 3389, which is a critical security risk. To fix this, we need to restrict the access to only trusted IP addresses or CIDR blocks. By updating the security group rule to include a specific CIDR block, we can prevent unauthorized access to the RDP port.
findings.fix_hint: Restrict the security group rule to only allow RDP access from trusted IP addresses or CIDR blocks
findings.fixed_code: aws_security_group_rule.app_sg_rule { from_port = 3389 to_port = 3389 protocol = "tcp" type = "ingress" cidr_blocks = ["192.168.1.0/24"] }

findings.title: Security group allows unrestricted SSH (port 22)
findings.description: The security group allows unrestricted access to port 22, which is a critical vulnerability. To fix this, we need to restrict the ingress rule to only allow SSH access from trusted IP addresses or CIDR blocks. By updating the security group resource, we can limit the exposure to only trusted sources.
findings.fix_hint: Restrict the security group to only allow SSH access from trusted IP addresses or CIDR blocks

findings.title: S3 bucket allows public policy

findings.title: IAM policy allows wildcard resource (*)
findings.description: The current IAM policy allows access to all resources in the account due to the wildcard (*) in the Resource field, which is a critical security risk. To fix this, the policy should be updated to only allow access to specific, necessary resources. This can be achieved by replacing the wildcard with an array of explicit ARNs, as shown in the fixed code snippet.
findings.fix_hint: Update the IAM policy to specify explicit resources instead of using a wildcard (*)

findings.title: Admin Managed Policy: AdministratorAccess
findings.description: The current policy grants unrestricted AWS access, violating the principle of least privilege. A custom policy should be created to only grant necessary permissions for the AppLambdaRole, such as lambda execution and logging. This can be achieved by replacing the AdministratorAccess policy with a custom policy, such as the LambdaExecutionRolePolicy.
findings.fix_hint: Replace the AdministratorAccess policy with a custom policy that only grants necessary permissions for the AppLambdaRole

findings.title: Dangerous IAM action: iam:*
findings.description: The current policy grants full IAM control, which is a critical security risk. To fix this, we need to replace the 'iam:*' action with specific required actions, such as 'iam:PassRole', 'iam:GetRole', and 'iam:ListRoles', to limit the privileges granted to the DeployUser. This change ensures that the policy only allows necessary actions, reducing the risk of privilege escalation.
findings.fix_hint: Replace the 'iam:*' action with specific required actions in the AppInlinePolicy

findings.title: Privilege Escalation Path Detected
findings.description: The original policy allows the DeployUser to create a Lambda function with any role, which is a privilege escalation path. The fixed policy restricts the DeployUser to only create Lambda functions and pass the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole, which is a more limited and secure set of permissions. This change prevents the DeployUser from creating a Lambda function with an admin role and executing arbitrary code as an administrator.
findings.fix_hint: Restrict the AppInlinePolicy to only allow necessary actions and resources

findings.title: Dangerous IAM action: *
findings.description: The current policy grants all AWS permissions to all resources, which is a critical security risk. To fix this, we need to specify the exact actions required by the lambda function, such as logging actions. By doing so, we limit the permissions to only what is necessary, reducing the attack surface.
findings.fix_hint: Replace the wildcard action with a specific set of actions required by the lambda function

findings.title: Admin Policy Reference: AdministratorAccess
findings.description: The AdministratorAccess policy grants full AWS access, which is a security risk. A custom policy should be created to include only the necessary permissions, such as logging, for the lambda execution role. This fix replaces the AdministratorAccess policy with a custom policy that includes only the necessary permissions.
findings.fix_hint: Replace the AdministratorAccess policy with a custom policy that includes only the necessary permissions for the lambda execution role

findings.fix_hint: Automated fix unavailable — review manually.

findings.title: Rds Insecure Password Storage In Source Code
findings.description: The hardcoded password in the aws_db_instance resource is a security risk, as it can be accessed by anyone with access to the Terraform configuration files. To fix this, a random password can be generated using the random_password resource and passed to the aws_db_instance resource. This ensures that the password is not stored in plain text and is unique for each deployment.
findings.fix_hint: Use the aws_db_instance resource with a random password generated by the random_password resource
findings.fixed_code:
resource "aws_db_instance" "app_db" {
  identifier             = "app-database"
  engine                 = "mysql"
  engine_version         = "8.0"
  instance_class         = "db.t3.micro"
  allocated_storage      = 20
  db_name                = "appdb"
  username               = "admin"
  password               = random_password.app_db_password.result
  publicly_accessible    = true
  skip_final_snapshot    = true
  storage_encrypted      = false
  deletion_protection    = false
}

resource "random_password" "app_db_password" {
  length = 16
  special = true
}

By using a parameterized query, the execute method will treat the user input as a literal value instead of part of the SQL code, preventing the injection. This fix assumes that the sqlite3 library is being used, which supports parameterized queries with the '?' placeholder.
findings.cwe: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
findings.fix_hint: Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection by passing user input as a parameter to the execute method instead of directly formatting it into the query string

findings.title: Avoid_App_Run_With_Bad_Host
findings.description: Running the Flask app with host 0.0.0.0 makes it accessible from outside the local machine, posing a security risk. Changing the host to 127.0.0.1 restricts access to the local machine only. Additionally, debug mode is disabled to prevent exposure of full stack traces in production.
findings.cwe: CWE-668: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere
findings.fix_hint: Change the host from 0.0.0.0 to 127.0.0.1 to prevent public exposure of the server

findings.title: Debug Enabled

findings.fix_hint: Set the debug mode to False or configure it using environment variables

findings.title: Direct Response Write
findings.description: The original code directly writes user input to the response object, making it vulnerable to XSS attacks. To fix this, we use a template engine like EJS to render the HTML and automatically escape user input. This ensures that any user-provided data is safely escaped and cannot be executed as code.
findings.cwe: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
findings.fix_hint: Use template engine to render HTML and escape user input
findings.fixed_code: function renderProfile(req, res) { const name = req.query.name; res.render('profile', { name: name }); }

findings.title: Raw Html Format
findings.description: The current implementation directly interpolates user input into the HTML response, making it vulnerable to XSS attacks. Sanitizing the input using DOMPurify prevents malicious code from being executed. This fix assumes that the DOMPurify library is installed and imported in the code.
findings.cwe: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
findings.fix_hint: Use a templating engine or a library like DOMPurify to sanitize user input before rendering it in HTML

attack_chains.title: Cloud Infrastructure Takeover
attack_chains.description: An attacker gains access to the cloud infrastructure by exploiting hardcoded AWS credentials in the code, then uses the unrestricted security group rules to access the RDS instance and exfiltrate sensitive data.
steps: Step 1: attacker reads hardcoded AWS access key and secret using finding f5d7bd56 in file xentinel-demo-repo/src/app.py
Step 2: this gives them access to the cloud infrastructure, which they use to exploit finding e032de32 in file uploaded_repo/xentinel-demo-repo/infra/main.tf to access the RDS instance
attack_chains.remediation: Remove hardcoded AWS credentials from the code and store them securely using AWS Secrets Manager

attack_chains.title: Privilege Escalation and Data Exfiltration
attack_chains.description: An attacker escalates privileges by exploiting a SQL injection vulnerability in the code, then uses the elevated privileges to access sensitive data in the S3 bucket and exfiltrate it.
steps: Step 1: attacker exploits SQL injection vulnerability using finding 33b2a3e7 in file xentinel-demo-repo/src/auth.js
Step 2: this gives them elevated privileges, which they use to exploit finding b7c5b288 in file uploaded_repo/xentinel-demo-repo/infra/main.tf to access the S3 bucket
attack_chains.remediation: Implement input validation and sanitization to prevent SQL injection attacks

attack_chains.title: Code Execution and Cloud Infrastructure Access
attack_chains.description: An attacker gains code execution on the server by exploiting a subprocess injection vulnerability, then uses the code execution to access the cloud infrastructure and exploit an unrestricted security group rule to access the EC2 instance.
steps: Step 1: attacker exploits subprocess injection vulnerability using finding c9830087 in file xentinel-demo-repo/src/app.py
Step 2: this gives them code execution on the server, which they use to exploit finding 0d1b2418 in file uploaded_repo/xentinel-demo-repo/infra/main.tf to access the EC2 instance
attack_chains.remediation: Implement secure coding practices to prevent subprocess injection attacks
